newsitem.title: USA: Malcolm X grandson sent to U.S. juvenile center.
newsitem.headline: Malcolm X grandson sent to U.S. juvenile center.

text.p: A judge on Friday ordered the grandson of slain U.S. black rights advocate Malcolm X to spend at least 18 months in a juvenile detention facility for starting a fire that killed his grandmother.
A Family Court judge in Yonkers, New York, ordered 12-year-old Malcolm Shabazz held at the Hillcrest Educational Centre in Lenox, Mass. The 18-month term may be extended until he is 18 years old.
Young Shabazz will be sent to Hillcrest on or before Aug 25, the judge said.

The boy pleaded guilty last month to setting the fire that killed 63-year-old Betty Shabazz. She died on June 23 from burns she suffered in the June 1 blaze at her apartment in Yonkers, a suburb north of New York City.

"You have a challenging road ahead," Family Court Judge Howard Spitz told the boy. "I know you have have the ability to prevail and become an outstanding citizen who can contribute to society. Good luck and Godspeed."
He also told him he suffered from "a mental illness."

Shabazz sat motionless and betrayed no emotion as the judge spoke. In custody since setting the fire, he arrived at the courthouse with his face covered and in shackles that caused him to stumble as he walked.

Experts have testified at court hearings that he has had a long and unusual interest in fires, set a blaze when he was a toddler and fantasized about an imaginary cartoon character he named "Sinister Torch."
Experts also testified he was the victim of abuse.
At the start of Friday's hearing, Dr. Don Heacock, a consultant to the court, said: "His morale is good, and he is looking forward to getting on with his life."

The Hillcrest facility was not the one preferred by Shabazz family members, longtime family friend and former New York City Mayor David Dinkins and attorney Percy Sutton, who argued to have the boy sent to a facility in Virginia.
However, an expert for the prosecution testified that the Pines facility in Portsmouth, Virgnia, had a high escape rate and reports of fires being set by children staying there.
A disappointed Dinkins said afterward he had not been aware of problems at the Virgnia facility and would not have supported it if he had known.

During the hearing, the boy's mother, Qubilah Shabazz, sat near her son and frequently stroked his hand. She is one of six daughters of Betty Shabazz and Malcolm X, who was assassinated in Harlem in 1965.
Testifying from Hillcrest was Dr. Jane Miller, who said the facility's goal would be to reduce the risk of the boy's "fire-setting" and "assaultive" behaviour.
Children at the centre are under constant supervision, she said, and another doctor said the facility had a "99 percent" success rate with children who set fires.
Sutton objected that Hillcrest was "dreary" and "falling down."
"It is the best institution available as determined by law," the judge said.
